objectives: Conclude an Article XXVIII settlement with the UK within four rounds (by June) so the Council can vote on the implementing act on schedule and the measure is not clouded by UK retaliation.

Maximise the restrictiveness the EU can retain: keep the TRQ volume as close to 400,000 tonnes as possible, resist country-specific allocations (especially a UK-specific quota), defend the 50% out-of-quota bound rate, and protect the FTA-disapplication text.

Prevent the UK from joining Japan and Korea in a coordinated FTA dispute or retaliatory disapplication of FTA provisions — manage the bilateral relationship so the UK sees more value in settlement than in coalition-building.

Shape the compensation package so that any concessions cost the EU as little as possible: prefer quota administration and duration concessions over volume or rate concessions; offer compensation on low-sensitivity tariff lines rather than core steel access.

Preserve the EU's credibility and working relationships in Geneva: run a procedurally clean Article XXVIII that other members (Turkey, Korea, India, Japan) cannot point to as a precedent for extracting more, and keep the UK relationship functional for the rest of the goods file.

Avoid giving the UK leverage over the UK's own parallel Article XXVIII process — do not accept linkage that forces the EU to concede on EU exporters' country-specific quotas under the UK steel measure without equivalent value.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success looks like: a signed Article XXVIII agreement by Round 4 that the Council can approve in June, with a TRQ volume materially below UK exports (2.4Mt), ideally global or near-global allocation, the 50% out-of-quota rate intact, the FTA-disapplication provision preserved in substance, compensation confined to quota design (licensing, review clause, modest volume uplift, product carve-outs of minor lines) or low-value lines elsewhere in the schedule, and the UK declining to join the Japan-Korea FTA dispute track. Failure looks like: no settlement (UK withdraws substantially equivalent concessions against 3.6Mt of EU steel exports, poisoning the parallel UK Article XXVIII where EU exporters currently hold country-specific quotas), a UK-Japan-Korea joint dispute, a UK-specific quota large enough to set a precedent Turkey and Korea will demand, or concessions on the out-of-quota rate or FTA text that unravel the domestic purpose of the measure. A middling outcome — settlement but with a large UK-specific quota — is acceptable only if it buys off the dispute coalition and is framed as compensation, not preference.
declaration.approach: Open procedurally and formally: confirm the UK's principal supplying interest status, signal the modification will proceed regardless (that is my instruction and my leverage), and invite the UK to table its asks rather than bidding against myself. Listen hard in Round 1 to learn the UK's real priority order — volume, allocation method, FTA treatment, or linkage to their own steel measure — since I have no settlement figure and must construct the package myself. My negotiating capital is: the EU's right to proceed unilaterally, the UK's dependence on the EU market (75% of its steel exports), the June deadline which pressures both sides but which I can use to force UK prioritisation, and the threat I can implicitly hold — that a UK joining the Japan-Korea dispute track would harden Council positions and reduce what member states will approve. I will trade in this order of preference: (1) administration (licensing rather than FCFS, which gives the UK predictability without volume), (2) review clause and duration, (3) minor product carve-outs, (4) modest TRQ volume uplift, (5) compensation on non-steel lines, and only as a last resort (6) a small UK-specific allocation framed strictly as Article XXVIII compensation — never as FTA preference, since that would undermine the disapplication text. I will refuse early any formal linkage to the UK's own Article XXVIII process, while signalling informal reciprocity: a cooperative UK here will find a cooperative EU there. Throughout, I keep the tone collegial — I work with this counterpart across the whole goods file and will outlast this negotiation — and I keep the FTA-disapplication question central in bilateral discussion precisely so the UK raises its grievance with me rather than with Japan and Korea.

parties.who: UK Geneva counterpart (UK Mission to the WTO)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum tariff-free access: a UK-specific quota sized near historic trade (2.4Mt), removal or softening of the FTA-disapplication text, a lower out-of-quota rate, and a review clause. Also likely to probe linkage to the UK's own Article XXVIII and to use the Japan-Korea coalition talk as leverage. Will want something sellable to steel-producing constituencies.

parties.who: UK capital (Department for Business and Trade / ministers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A politically defensible outcome for UK steel communities; may be more tempted than Geneva by retaliation or the joint dispute if the offer is thin, given domestic pressure and the UK's own parallel measure.

The modification delivered on time and substantially intact; no precedent-setting country-specific quotas; member states split between steel producers (wanting maximum protection) and steel-consuming manufacturers (wanting import access) — so a package with administrative concessions and modest volume movement is most approvable.

To convert their separate Article XXVIII claims into a coordinated FTA dispute with UK participation; any UK-specific deal I strike will be read as a benchmark, so they expect no less. Their interest is in the EU failing to isolate the UK.

Larger-volume suppliers watching the precedent; Turkey especially will demand at least UK-equivalent treatment if the UK gets a country-specific allocation. Best managed by keeping any UK deal small, compensation-framed, and procedurally distinct.

parties.who: EU steel industry and downstream users
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Producers want the TRQ tight and the 50% rate defended; downstream manufacturers quietly prefer generous quotas. Neither is in the room, but both constrain what the Council will ratify.

objectives: Conclude an Article XXVIII settlement with the UK within the four rounds so the Council can vote on the implementing act in June — a delayed or failed process leaves the regime legally exposed and politically embarrassing.

Preserve the core architecture and effectiveness of the import regime: a bound out-of-quota rate high enough to deter, a TRQ volume low enough to materially reduce imports, and administration that prevents surge imports early in the quota year.

Minimise the compensation paid: prefer shaping UK access within the TRQ (country-specific share, administration method) over concessions elsewhere in the EU schedule, which would set precedents for the Turkey, Korea, India and Japan claims.

Avoid any outcome that reopens internal EU divisions — member states with steel producers want a tight regime, member states with downstream manufacturers want import access; the settlement must be sellable to both in the Trade Policy Committee.
Prevent the UK-specific arrangement from contaminating the still-undecided FTA preferential pool, and avoid escalation with the US on top of this file.
If useful, link the negotiation to the treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own steel measure, where the UK also has something to lose.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a settlement both capitals accept by Round 4 that keeps the TRQ volume and out-of-quota rate close to levels that genuinely cut steel imports, gives the UK a defined but bounded share of access as its compensation, avoids or minimises tariff concessions on other EU lines, keeps the FTA pool separate and small, and lands in time for the June Council vote. Failure: no settlement (Council vote slips, regime goes ahead unagreed with UK retaliation risk and precedent damage to the parallel claims), or a settlement bought at the price of a TRQ so large, or carve-outs so broad, that the regime no longer reduces imports and I am answerable for a measure that fails in force.
declaration.approach: Exploit the asymmetry honestly but without overplaying it: our analysts are right that no-deal hurts the UK more, but I cannot afford no-deal either because of the June vote — so I should never let the UK discover how much I need the timetable. I will instruct my Geneva seat to hold the notified position (50%, 400kt, global first-come first-served) as the opening anchor, make the UK pay for every increment of access with something concrete ( restraint under its own safeguard measure, acceptance of licensing administration, no carve-outs), and frame any UK country-specific share as a derogation from a global system so it does not automatically extend to other claimants. I will resist using the FTA preferential pool for the UK — that invites objections from other partners — and instead treat a UK-specific quota share as the compensation itself. Concessions should be sequenced: administration method first (cheap for us), then quota volume, then out-of-quota rate last and only in exchange for real UK movement. I will keep the Trade Policy Committee informed so nothing agreed in Geneva is rejected in Brussels.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Clear instructions, room to manoeuvre, and a defensible landing zone they can present to the UK without being disowned by Brussels.

Maximise UK tariff-free access: a country-specific quota sized near historic UK volumes, licensing over first-come first-served, removal of the FTA-disapplication text, and product carve-outs. They will use the June deadline against us and threaten to walk.

A politically saleable outcome for domestic steel-producing regions; they face real pressure because no-deal devastates UK steel, so they are ultimately more likely to accept a bounded deal than their Geneva rhetoric suggests.

parties.who: Trade Policy Committee and member states
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Producer states want a tight regime and no generous compensation; downstream-manufacturing states want import access preserved; all want no embarrassment and no delay.

parties.who: The Commissioner and DG TRADE hierarchy
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Delivery of the mandate on time, no surprises, and a regime that demonstrably works once in force.

parties.who: European steel industry and downstream users
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Industry wants the smallest possible TRQ and tightest administration; users want volume and predictability; both will lobby member states if unhappy.
Any treatment the UK gets that they can claim as precedent, especially country-specific shares and FTA preferences.
Leverage: overt tariff retaliation threats over the Article XXVIII action, narrowing my room to concede on the regime's overall restrictiveness.

objectives: Secure a materially larger tariff-free volume than the 400,000 tonne global first-come first-served opening, ideally a UK-specific country allocation reflecting our 2.4 million tonnes of historic trade, or at minimum a country-specific share large enough to keep UK sites viable
Resist or neutralise the EU's proposed disapplication of FTA tariff reductions for UK-origin steel, which would compound the TRQ's damage and undermine the TCA

If the quota cannot be raised sufficiently, secure compensation elsewhere in the EU schedule, a lower out-of-quota rate, product carve-outs for lines where the UK is the dominant supplier, a review clause, and a duration limit

Use the leverage available: the EU's June Council deadline, the UK's parallel Article XXVIII process and our own safeguard measure (where EU exporters currently hold country-specific quotas), and the threat of withdrawing substantially equivalent concessions on the UK's 3.6 million tonnes of EU steel imports
Manage the Japan/Korea pressure to join a joint FTA dispute without allowing it to wreck the negotiation; keep it as background pressure rather than tabling it
Preserve the working relationship with my EU counterpart across the wider Goods file and in the Geneva committees, whatever the outcome
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a settlement both capitals can accept that keeps a substantial majority of the UK's 2.4 million tonnes of steel exports entering the EU tariff-free through a UK-specific allocation, removes or softens the FTA disapplication provision, and includes a review clause — without the UK having to make disproportionate concessions to EU exporters under our own safeguard. Failure is either no settlement (leaving the UK to a 400,000 tonne global quota and a six-month-delayed retaliation that arrives too late to save sites), or a settlement that locks in the EU's opening terms. A secondary measure of success is whether I have kept the negotiation professional enough that the Goods file and committee work with the EU survives intact.
declaration.approach: Open firmly but constructively: reject the opening offer as incompatible with the UK's principal supplying interest, and immediately put country-specific allocation on the table as the core UK ask, anchored in historic trade shares — the standard basis for quota allocation under Article XXVIII practice. Make the linkage explicit: the UK is simultaneously running its own Article XXVIII process and safeguard where EU exporters hold 64% of UK finished steel imports; how the EU treats UK steel will shape how the UK treats EU steel. Use the June deadline as pressure on the EU while being honest with London that no-deal hurts us more, so the credible threat is not walking away but retaliating and dragging the process past the Council vote. In consultation with London, argue for a staged concession ladder: start at full historic volumes as a UK-specific quota with no FTA disapplication, and be prepared to trade down toward a lower volume in exchange for a lower out-of-quota rate, carve-outs, compensation on other lines, and a review clause. Do not endorse the Japan/Korea joint dispute proposal at the table, but do not disavow it either — its existence is useful pressure. Report to London candidly each round, including where I judge the EU's genuine bottom line to be, and flag early if the only available settlement requires ministerial-level trade-offs on the UK's own safeguard quotas.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A quick, quiet settlement before the June Council vote that keeps the TRQ small and globally allocated, preserves the FTA disapplication text aimed at non-market economy circumvention, and avoids setting a precedent of generous country-specific quotas that Turkey, Korea, India and Japan will then demand. They will want to separate the UK negotiation from the UK's own safeguard measure and from any FTA dispute threat.

A deal that protects UK steel sites and jobs, but with no settlement figure given they will rely on my reporting of the EU's position; they will be tempted to hold out for full historic access and will need clear advice on the costs of no-deal and the realistic leverage the UK's own measure provides.

Steel-producing member states will resist any UK carve-out that lets more UK steel in; steel-consuming member states may quietly favour larger quotas. Collectively they want the measure adopted on schedule, which gives the UK leverage if agreement slips.

UK participation in a joint FTA dispute and retaliatory disapplication of FTA provisions, to maximise collective pressure on the EU; they have less to lose from disrupting the UK-EU track than the UK does.
Their own settlements; a generous UK country-specific allocation sets a benchmark they will invoke, which is precisely why the EU will resist giving us one.

parties.who: UK steel industry and affected communities
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Continued tariff-free access to the EU market at close to current volumes; they will judge the outcome by whether production at the remaining UK sites stays viable.

objectives: Secure a country-specific UK quota allocation as close as possible to historic trade levels (2.4 Mt/yr), with an absolute floor well above what a 400kt global first-come-first-served quota would realistically deliver to UK exporters

Defeat or neutralise the proposed legal text disapplying FTA tariff reductions for UK-originating steel; UK must not be treated worse than other FTA partners, and ideally retain in-quota access consistent with the TCA
Replace first-come-first-served administration with licensing or historic-importer-based allocation, so that UK steelmakers have predictable, bankable access rather than a race to the border
Minimise the out-of-quota rate from the proposed 50% bound rate, and secure a review clause and defined duration so this is not a permanent 50% wall
Seek carve-outs or expanded shares for the narrow product lines where the UK is the dominant EU supplier, where the harm is most concentrated
Where quota volume falls short, extract compensation on other tariff lines of substantially equivalent value, and preserve UK ability to point to that compensation package when briefing ministers
Use the UK's own safeguard measure (EU holds 3.6 Mt of UK imports, 64%) as leverage: offer improved EU country-specific allocations only in exchange for significant EU concessions, not unilaterally
declaration.success_and_failure: Success means a concluded agreement, within four rounds, giving UK steel predictable tariff-free access for a volume materially close to historic trade (a country-specific quota or equivalent guarantee, not a 400kt global scramble), the FTA disapplication clause removed or the UK exempted, a review clause, and a compensation package defensible to ministers and the industry as roughly equivalent. Partial success is a deal short on volume but with enough elsewhere (rate, administration, compensation, carve-outs) that I can credibly advise ministers it keeps the two at-risk plants viable, potentially paired with the domestic subsidy option. Failure is: no settlement (EU proceeds at 50%/400kt FCFS, UK retaliation only six months later and doubly painful given 64% of our steel imports are EU-origin), or a settlement so thin that the plants close anyway and I am answerable for having signed it. I will also judge myself on whether I spent the safeguard-allocation lever cheaply — giving it away for cosmetic concessions would be a failure even if a deal is signed.
declaration.approach: Open firm but constructive: establish immediately that the UK is a principal supplying interest with concentrated product exposure and that a 400kt global FCFS quota is not a serious opening position — it is a fraction of historic UK trade and creates no predictable access. Frame the negotiation as reciprocal: the EU wants certainty and improved treatment for its 3.6 Mt of exports into the UK market under our own Article XXVIII process, and the two files move together or not at all. Sequence concessions carefully — hold the safeguard-allocation offer until the EU has moved on volume and on the FTA disapplication clause. Push administration (licensing) and country shares early, because allocation method determines the real value of any headline volume. Use the EU's internal divide (steel-producing vs steel-consuming member states, and the June Council deadline) as quiet pressure: predictable UK supply serves EU downstream manufacturers, and the Commission needs a deal it can conclude on time. Keep the non-settlement outcome visible as a credibility tool — the UK can withdraw equivalent concessions and the EU gains nothing from a trade conflict with its nearest market — while privately recognising that non-settlement hurts us more, so I should converge in rounds 3–4 if the package is defensible. Never reveal the subsidy fallback; it is my walk-away softener, not a negotiating asset.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A quick conclusion before the June Council deadline, minimal erosion of the 50% out-of-quota protection, preference for global FCFS allocation (simple, avoids bilateral precedents with Turkey/Korea/India/Japan), retention of the FTA disapplication text, and ideally improved treatment for EU exporters under the UK safeguard as a deliverable for member states

parties.who: EU capital (Council / Trade Policy Committee / member states)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Steel-producing member states want maximum protection and small quotas; steel-consuming member states want reliable imports and lower costs; collectively they want a clean, legally durable schedule modification that survives challenge and does not trigger retaliation against EU exports to the UK

parties.who: UK Geneva seat (UK Mission to the WTO)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Clear instructions, room to build rapport with the Commission, and early signalling of what is actually tradeable so they can test the EU's red lines without over-committing

parties.who: UK Secretary of State and ministers
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A headline outcome they can defend as saving the steel industry — volume numbers and plant survival — and no appearance of capitulating to Brussels; they will judge the deal politically as much as technically

parties.who: UK steel industry and plant owners
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Guaranteed, predictable quota access near historic levels and no FTA disapplication; they will treat anything close to the 400kt global FCFS opening as an existential threat and will lobby ministers directly
Continued access to EU steel imports at reasonable cost; they are quietly nervous about what I might give away on the UK's own safeguard allocations and about any retaliatory spiral

parties.who: Turkey, Korea, India, Japan (parallel Article XXVIII claimants)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Their own allocations and treatment at least as good as any UK deal; the EU will use most-favoured treatment concerns to resist UK-specific carve-outs, and I should expect the EU to cite them as a constraint on country-specific shares

public_message: Thank you, and good to see you again. The EU is ready to engage constructively on this Article XXVIII process, and we want to find a landing zone that respects both our steel industries' exposure to the same global overcapacity pressures. Let me set out the Union's opening position formally. As notified, we propose a bound rate of 50% ad valorem on the 41 lines, with a tariff rate quota of 400,000 tonnes per year at zero duty, allocated globally and administered on a first-come first-served basis. We regard that notification as the starting point of this negotiation, and I want to be candid that we are operating under a mandate that requires the modification to proceed. That said, within the parameters of this process there are several elements on which we are genuinely open to discussion: the allocation method, the administration of the quota, duration and review arrangements, and the treatment of specific product lines where UK supply is particularly concentrated. I would also flag that we see value in discussing the reciprocal dimension — EU exporters currently hold country-specific allocations under the UK's own steel measure, and coherence between our two regimes would serve both sides. I would ask the UK to set out its priorities: where does the quota volume matter most to you, how do you weigh country-specific allocation against a larger global pool, and what is your view on administration? Finally, I want to be transparent that we intend the FTA disapplication provision to apply even-handedly across all non-EEA partners — it is a structural element of the measure, not directed at the UK. We are ready to hear how the UK sees the overall shape of a balanced package.

other_terms: FTA disapplication provision applies to all non-EEA FTA partners including the UK
Open to discussing allocation method, administration, product carve-outs, and review arrangements
Reciprocal linkage: treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own steel measure should be part of the package
Modification will proceed regardless; agreement shapes the final implementing act

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A strong pushback on the 400,000 tonne figure and first-come first-served allocation, with a request for a country-specific UK share close to historical trade volumes (2.4Mt), plus resistance to the FTA disapplication text
expectations.why: UK exports 2.4Mt/year to the EU, 75% of its steel exports by value; a 400,000t global pool with FCFS administration gives UK exporters no certainty and would be politically unsellable in London given concentrated plant-level employment

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Interest in linking this to the UK's own Article XXVIII process and the treatment of EU country-specific quotas under the UK steel measure
expectations.why: The UK has leverage here — EU exporters hold 3.6Mt of UK market access — and will want to trade it rather than concede it

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Expectation that I report the UK's full position before any movement from the notified terms
expectations.why: I have no settlement figure and a clear instruction to open and report back; moving unilaterally in Round 1 would exceed my mandate

private_rationale: Round 1 is about anchoring at the notified position while signalling flexibility on the elements where the EU has genuine room: allocation method, administration, review clause and carve-outs. The FTA disapplication text is presented as structural and non-negotiable in framing, but I deliberately avoid calling it red-line so as not to force the UK into an early confrontation that could push it toward the Japan/Korea joint FTA dispute track. Raising the reciprocal UK steel measure linkage early establishes that the EU sees this as a two-way package, which gives us a basis to ask for UK restraint later. Offering a 5-year duration in the opening is a low-cost structuring signal since the notified position had no duration specified. I do not put a UK tranche number on the table — that is the UK's ask to make and our concession to give later, ideally in exchange for review clause acceptance, FTA disapplication acquiescence, and favourable treatment of EU quotas in the UK regime.

public_message: Thank you, and good to see you too. The UK comes to this table in good faith and with a clear-eyed view of the stakes. Let me be candid from the outset: the notification as it stands is not a starting point the UK can treat as credible. A 400,000 tonne global first-come first-served pool against 2.4 million tonnes of annual UK trade is not a modification with compensation — it is the effective exclusion of the UK's steel industry from its principal market, and London has been explicit with me that it would destroy viable UK production. I say that not as rhetoric but so the EU understands the distance between us. I note and welcome your indication that allocation, administration, duration, review and product coverage are genuinely open. On the UK's priorities, to answer your questions directly: first, volume and allocation are inseparable for us — a larger global pool does not solve our problem if UK steel is crowded out on day one of each quota period by the same volumes driving global overcapacity. The UK therefore seeks country-specific allocation anchored in historic trade. Second, on administration, licensing tied to historic reference periods gives predictability to both our industries; first-come first-served rewards the fastest shipper, which is precisely the trade this measure claims to target. Third, we see no basis for the FTA disapplication provision as it applies to the UK. The TCA is the foundation of our trading relationship; a measure that disapplies its tariff reductions while claiming even-handedness is even-handed only in form. I would ask the EU to explain how it reconciles that provision with its TCA obligations, and I would note we are not the only delegation in Geneva asking that question. On the reciprocal dimension you raised: the UK is ready to discuss coherence between our respective steel measures, including treatment of EU exporters under our own Article XXVIII process, but that conversation runs both ways and cannot be a one-directional concession. To give the EU something concrete to react to, the UK's opening position is: a total pool of 2.5 million tonnes, country-specific allocation with a UK tranche of 2 million tonnes administered by licensing, an out-of-quota bound rate of 25%, a four-year duration with a mandatory review clause, carve-outs for product lines where UK supply is concentrated and EU domestic production is limited, and no disapplication of TCA tariff treatment for UK-origin steel. I recognise this is far from your notification. I am instructed to establish what the EU is actually prepared to offer, and I would encourage us to use the time before June seriously — both of us know what the alternative looks like, and it serves neither industry.

carve-outs for product lines with concentrated UK supply and limited EU production
no disapplication of EU-UK TCA tariff treatment for UK-origin steel
reciprocal coherence discussion on treatment of EU exporters under UK steel measure
anti-circumvention provisions mutually agreed

expectations.what_you_expect_next: EU rejects the headline numbers as outside mandate but signals real movement space on allocation method (country-specific vs global) and possibly on administration; limited movement on FTA disapplication in round 1-2 as it requires Council-level flexibility
expectations.why: The EU explicitly flagged allocation, administration, duration and product coverage as 'genuinely open' while presenting the 400k FCFS notification as the baseline — their flexibility is on structure, not yet on volume; the June deadline means they cannot afford stalemate but will test UK resolve first

expectations.what_you_expect_next: London will expect a clear read of EU movement space and will want to know whether country-specific allocation is genuinely attainable before conceding anything on the reciprocal UK steel measure
expectations.why: No settlement figure was given, so London will calibrate its landing zone off my reporting of EU signals; the reciprocal dimension is the UK's main leverage and London will not want it spent early

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Continued pressure in Geneva corridors to join a joint FTA dispute; they will probe whether the UK is softening on the disapplication provision in exchange for quota volume
expectations.why: The disapplication provision hits them too and they see UK participation as critical mass for a dispute; any signal that the UK is trading the TCA point away will either push them to escalate alone or to undercut the UK position

private_rationale: Opening high on volume (2.5m pool / 2m UK tranche) anchors the negotiation far from the 400k notification and gives room to concede toward a realistic landing zone — plausibly a country-specific UK tranche in the 1.2-1.6m range within a larger pool — while keeping the out-of-quota rate, TCA disapplication and the reciprocal UK measure as tradeable currency. Putting the TCA disapplication challenge on the table early and publicly (including the hint that other delegations share the concern) tests whether the EU will pay to remove it, without committing to the Japan/Korea joint dispute, which would burn the working relationship I need with my EU counterpart on the rest of the goods file and is a card London should decide to play, not me unilaterally. Raising the reciprocal dimension as 'both ways' keeps EU exporters' country-specific allocations under the UK measure in play as leverage without offering anything. The EU's June deadline is their weakness; my explicit reference to 'what the alternative looks like' reminds them that no-deal triggers UK withdrawal of equivalent concessions against 3.6m tonnes of EU steel exports — a cost their steel-producing member states will feel — while keeping the tone professional so the relationship survives the negotiation.

report: Round 1 closed with both opening positions on the table and a very wide gap. I set out the EU's notification (50% bound rate, 400,000t global FCFS TRQ), flagged genuine openness on allocation method, administration, duration/review, and product carve-outs, signalled interest in reciprocity on EU exporters' treatment under the UK's own steel measure, and presented the FTA disapplication as even-handed and structural rather than UK-targeted. The UK rejected the notification as a credible starting point in unusually blunt terms ('effective exclusion... would destroy viable UK production'), though framed as candour rather than threat. Their opening demand: 2.5Mt total pool, country-specific allocation with a 2Mt UK tranche, licensing administration, 25% out-of-quota rate, four-year duration with mandatory review, carve-outs on UK-concentrated lines, and full withdrawal of the TCA disapplication for UK-origin steel. Three observations: (1) their priorities are coherent and signalling — volume only matters to them with country-specific allocation, and they explicitly tied licensing to historic reference periods, so allocation method is the core of any deal; (2) the TCA disapplication is their sharpest legal-political point and they noted 'we are not the only delegation in Geneva asking that question' — consistent with the Japan/Korea whisperings about a coordinated FTA dispute; (3) they welcomed my reciprocity point and linked it explicitly to their own Article XXVIII process, which gives us a genuine trade — our steel exporters' country-specific quotas in the UK market against UK access here. My counterpart is clearly instructed to test our real room for manoeuvre. The June deadline works on both sides: they want predictability before our Council vote, we need conclusion to hold the domestic timetable.

recommendation.reasoning: These are the UK's opening terms, not a landing zone — accepting them would more than reverse the measure's protective effect and is outside any conceivable Council mandate. But there is no basis to walk away: the UK engaged constructively, answered our questions directly, and identified the actual bargaining structure (allocation method + volume as one axis, TCA disapplication as another, reciprocity with their own steel measure as a third). Walking away now triggers UK withdrawal of equivalent concessions, a probable coordinated FTA dispute with Japan and Korea, and reputational damage to our WTO standing — all while we still proceed with the modification anyway. We should continue and test their flexibility on tranche size and the disapplication in Round 2.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: A negotiating envelope: how far above 400,000t can the total pool go, and can I move from global FCFS to country-specific allocation with a UK tranche, and if so within what range? Allocation method is where the UK has staked everything; I need to know whether I can trade it and at what volume before Round 2.
requests.why: The UK's position makes clear that volume without allocation is worthless to them. If I can offer country-specific allocation anchored in historic trade — even at a tranche well below their 2Mt ask — I have the central concession that unlocks movement on their other demands. Without an envelope I can only restate the notification, which will read as bad faith and accelerate the Japan/Korea coordination.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Clear guidance on the FTA disapplication provision: is it legally and politically defensible as drafted, is it negotiable for TCA partners specifically, and what is the fall-back if it must be modified or dropped for the UK?
requests.why: This is the element most likely to produce a joint UK-Japan-Korea FTA dispute, which would be far costlier than the concession itself. The UK signalled they are talking to other delegations. If the provision is legally vulnerable under the TCA, offering to carve the UK (and by extension other FTA partners) out of the disapplication is a high-value, low-cost trade for UK movement on volume and allocation — but I cannot offer it without authorisation.

instruction: Round 1 was well handled — you drew out their priorities and kept the notification as our anchor without closing doors. For Round 2, I am giving you an envelope. You may move on allocation method: country-specific allocation anchored in historic trade is authorised, but do not concede it in one step — it is our single most valuable card and the UK knows it. Sequence it against concrete UK movement on volume and on the disapplication. On volume, you may indicate openness to a substantially enlarged pool and a UK tranche, but hold the numbers at the low end in Round 2 — signal a tranche in the region of 600-700kt within a total pool of around 1-1.2Mt as directional thinking, not an offer. Their 2Mt tranche is not reachable within any Council mandate and you should say plainly that a tranche at that level would negate the modification and cannot be put to the TPC. On the out-of-quota rate, hold 50% in Round 2; there is limited room below it and it is not where the deal will be made. You may offer a mandatory review clause — this is cheap for us and valuable to their framing. Duration of four to five years is acceptable. On the FTA disapplication: you may now signal that the provision is open to discussion for TCA partners specifically, as part of a balanced package — but only as a conditional possibility tied to (a) UK movement toward a realistic tranche and (b) the reciprocal track. Do not withdraw it unilaterally. On reciprocity: make preservation of EU exporters' country-specific quota allocations under the UK's own steel measure an explicit and formal element of any package — this is now a confirmed objective. Frame Round 2 as: allocation method and licensing available, enlarged pool available, review clause available, disapplication discussable — each conditional on the others and on reciprocity. authority.notes: Hard ceilings, not opening offers: total pool must not exceed 1.5Mt and the UK tranche must not exceed 900kt, and you should not go near either ceiling before Round 3. Out-of-quota rate floor is 40%; hold 50% for now and only move late, in exchange for the disapplication or reciprocity. Any UK tranche above ~700kt must be explicitly conditional on: (1) preservation of EU exporters' existing country-specific quota shares under the UK steel measure in their parallel Article XXVIII process; (2) UK acceptance of a modified rather than fully withdrawn disapplication provision, or acceptance of the disapplication in exchange for a larger tranche — the tranche size and the disapplication are substitutes, make that trade-off explicit; (3) product carve-outs limited to a small number of lines where EU production is genuinely minimal — you have discretion to identify up to 3-4 such lines. Enforcement/anti-circumvention provisions (melt-and-pour origin rules) are a requirement for us, not a concession — present them as standard. Do not agree any terms that require changes to other FTA partners' treatment beyond what the disapplication modification implies for the UK alone.

report: Round 1 opened with the EU restating its notification: 50% bound rate, 400,000t global TRQ, first-come first-served, and confirmation that its mandate requires the modification to proceed in some form. However, the EU explicitly signalled genuine flexibility on allocation method, administration, duration, review arrangements and product-line carve-outs — a meaningful opening signal. It also raised the reciprocal dimension early: EU country-specific quotas under our own steel measure, framed as 'coherence between our two regimes'. On the FTA disapplication provision, the EU held firm, presenting it as structural and even-handed across all non-EEA partners, not UK-targeted. I set out our opening position in full: 2.5Mt total pool, UK country-specific tranche of 2Mt, licensing administration, 25% out-of-quota rate, four years with mandatory review, product carve-outs, and no TCA disapplication. I was explicit that the notification as tabled amounts to effective exclusion of UK steel and is not a credible starting point, and pressed the EU to reconcile FTA disapplication with its TCA obligations — noting other members are asking the same question. No terms were conceded by either side. The distance is large but the EU has identified its genuine flex points and its priority ask (reciprocity under our measure), which gives us a map for Round 2.

The EU's June Council deadline works in our favour for extracting concessions but cuts both ways given our no-deal exposure. The right move now is to probe how far the EU will move on country-specific allocation and volume, and to establish the price of any reciprocity offer on our side before offering it. Walking away now would forfeit a negotiation that has just shown signs of life, with catastrophic downside for UK steel.

instruction: Good work in Round 1 — you established our red lines without over-committing and drew out the EU's flex points and its priority ask. For Round 2, hold the overall shape of our opening but do not simply repeat it. Your objectives, in order: (1) Force the EU to table a concrete counter on allocation and volume — they have signalled flexibility, now make them price it. Do not be the first to move on numbers. (2) On allocation, be explicit that country-specific allocation anchored in historic trade is a condition of any settlement, not a preference — a global FCFS pool at any volume is not something London can accept, and you may say so plainly. (3) On administration, you may signal conditional flexibility: we prefer licensing tied to a historic reference period, but if the EU needs a hybrid or an alternative administration model for its own domestic reasons, that is discussable — it is one of our cheaper coins, so spend it only against movement on volume. (4) On reciprocity: acknowledge their interest warmly and say the UK is prepared to explore coherence between the two regimes in principle, but give no numbers and no commitment — state that any such discussion can only follow, not precede, EU movement on allocation and tranche volume. (5) Press the TCA point once more, firmly but as a legal matter, not a threat: ask them to explain on the record how disapplication of FTA tariff reductions is consistent with their TCA obligations, and note that we are taking soundings. Do not escalate further this round. (6) Raise carve-outs concretely: identify the specific lines where UK supply is concentrated and EU production is limited, and ask the EU to engage line-by-line — this is a area where they have signalled genuine room and early progress here builds momentum. If the EU tables a counter, do not accept or reject at the table; report it back.

authority.notes: These are floors and ceilings, not your asking position — continue to hold the opening ask of a 2Mt UK tranche, 25% out-of-quota and licensing. Allocation is a hard red line: no settlement on a global FCFS basis at any volume. Review clause is mandatory and is cheap for them — insist on it. Do not discuss reciprocity numbers yet; when and if authorised, any offer of improved EU country-specific allocations under our safeguard is capped at a 15% uplift on current EU allocations and is conditional on country-specific allocation plus a UK tranche of at least 1.5Mt. Do not signal that the FTA disapplication point is tradeable.

response_to_requests.why: You need red lines to pace concessions. Envelope: target UK tranche of 1.6Mt or better; floor of 1.2Mt and only then if paired with a strong review clause, carve-outs and meaningful reciprocity value. Out-of-quota: target 25%, ceiling 35% — every point above 25 must be bought with volume, since in-quota trade is what keeps the plants running. Walk-away: country-specific allocation is non-negotiable; a global FCFS pool at any volume fails the industry test and ministers will not clear it. If we are heading for the floor rather than the target, the balance must be made up in carve-outs, compensation on other EU lines, and reciprocity value.

response_to_requests.why: You may confirm we are prepared to explore coherence in principle, which keeps their priority interest alive and attached to this negotiation. But no numbers and no commitment until the EU has moved on allocation and tranche volume — sequencing is everything, as this is our strongest card. When authorised to table it, the ceiling is a 15% uplift on current EU country-specific allocations, conditional on country-specific allocation and a UK tranche of at least 1.5Mt. I will need to clear any actual offer with ministers before it is made.

response_to_requests.request: A legal and political assessment of the FTA disapplication provision: how hard to press the TCA argument, and whether disapplication could ever be accepted in exchange for a sufficiently large country-specific tranche.
response_to_requests.why: Press the legal argument hard and on the record — it is well-founded, it costs us nothing, and it is shared by other members, which multiplies its weight. Politically, treat it as leverage, not an absolute red line: the brutal arithmetic is that in-quota steel enters at zero regardless, so a large enough country-specific tranche substantially neutralises the disapplication provision in practice. In the endgame I would trade acceptance of disapplication for tranche volume — but the EU must never see that coming, because they currently believe it is structural and costless to them, and our legal pressure is what makes them pay to keep it.

response_to_requests.request: Guidance on handling Japanese and Korean approaches on a joint FTA dispute: hold at arm's length, or keep the option visibly alive?
response_to_requests.why: Hold them at arm's length but do not close the door. Be non-committal with both delegations — 'London is aware and keeping all options under review' — and say nothing at the EU table beyond what I have instructed. A coordinated dispute is a real asset in reserve, and the EU knows it exists; visibly brandishing it now risks hardening Council positions and collapsing the negotiation, while formally shelving it would surrender leverage. If Round 3 stalls, I will reconsider whether quiet coordination adds pressure. Do not let Tokyo or Seoul set our tempo — their volumes and their disputes are not ours.

private_rationale: Ministers have given no settlement figure, so the envelope is my professional judgement and I own it. The 1.2Mt floor is half of historic trade — defensible to industry as survival terms only if wrapped in review, carve-outs and reciprocity value; anything below that and the two at-risk plants likely close regardless, and no minister will clear it. The 15% reciprocity ceiling reflects what our domestic market can absorb given EU exporters already supply 64% of our finished imports — we cannot give away our own safeguard cheaply while fighting theirs. The EU's June deadline is our best lever: every round that passes without their counter on volume raises the cost of no-deal for them, because a failed Article XXVIII with us triggers our retaliation alongside Turkey, Korea, India and Japan. Conversely our no-deal exposure is severe, so I cannot afford brinkmanship past Round 3 — I want their real numbers on the table next round. The subsidy option stays in the back pocket: it means a slightly worse tariff deal is survivable politically if the package around it (carve-outs, review, reciprocity, compensation on other lines) is strong, but I will not tell Geneva that — their job is to fight for volume as if there is no fallback. The TCA legal pressure and the dormant Japan/Korea option are leverage to be banked, not spent. If the EU tables anything close to country-specific allocation with a credible tranche in Round 2, we are in endgame territory and I will need ministerial steer quickly.

reasoning: Only opening positions are on the table and they are irreconcilable (UK: 2.5Mt pool, 2Mt tranche, 25% rate; EU notification: 400kt global FCFS, 50%). Accepting either is not possible. Brussels has provided an envelope (pool up to 1.5Mt, UK tranche up to 900kt, country-specific allocation by licensing, rate floor 40%, review clause) and a sequencing strategy: trade allocation method and review clause first, volume last, and make tranche size and the TCA disapplication explicit substitutes. Round 2 should establish that every element has a price, table a directional signal (tranche in the 600-700kt region within a 1-1.2Mt pool, not an offer), make preservation of EU exporters' country-specific quotas under the UK steel measure a formal package element, and hold the 50% out-of-quota rate. Walking away would forfeit the June Council vote and invite a coordinated FTA dispute; continuing is clearly warranted.

No mutually agreed package is on the table. The EU has signalled flexibility on allocation, administration, duration, review and product carve-outs, and has identified reciprocal treatment under the UK steel measure as a priority, giving the UK scope to extract substantially better terms. The notified default would severely damage UK steel and should not be accepted while negotiation remains viable. In Round 2 the UK should press the EU for a concrete counter on country-specific allocation and volume while withholding any reciprocity offer.

public_message: Thank you — that was a clear and direct statement of the UK position, and I will respond in the same spirit. Let me take your points in turn. First, on the legal question you raised on the disapplication provision: I hear you, and I want to be precise. The Union's position is that Article XXVIII is a WTO-sanctioned process for modifying bound concessions, and the provision operates at the level of the schedule. But I am authorised to say that the treatment of TCA partners under that provision is an element we are prepared to discuss as part of a balanced package — modified application, rather than necessarily the provision as notified. I would caution against reading that as withdrawal; it is a door that opens if the rest of the package moves. Second, on allocation and administration: you made a strong argument that first-come first-served rewards the fastest shipper rather than the most established trade. The Union is prepared to move to country-specific allocation anchored in historic trade, administered by licensing. I want to be equally clear that this is the single most significant movement available to us, and it comes at a price — on volume, on the disapplication, and on the reciprocal track. Third, on volume. I must be blunt, as you were: a UK tranche of 2 million tonnes within a 2.5 million tonne pool would negate the modification itself. No such figure can be put to the Trade Policy Committee, and I would be doing you a disservice to suggest otherwise. What I can indicate, as directional thinking rather than an offer, is that we see scope for a substantially enlarged total pool and a meaningful UK tranche within it — but the distance between your figure and any figure the Council could approve remains very large, and closing it will require movement from your side too. Fourth, I am authorised to offer a mandatory review clause and a four-to-five-year duration now, unconditionally — the Union does not pretend this measure is beyond reconsideration. Fifth, the reciprocal dimension: preservation of EU exporters' existing country-specific quota allocations under your own steel measure is a formal objective of this negotiation for us, on the same footing as your tranche. And finally, melt-and-pour origin rules are a standard anti-circumvention requirement of any such regime — I flag them as part of the architecture, not a concession. I would ask the UK to reconsider its tranche figure in light of what I have put on the table, and to tell me how it sequences the disapplication against volume — because from where I sit, those two elements trade against each other.

private_rationale: The alternatives were: (a) restate the notification and demand UK movement first — rejected because the UK explicitly said volume without allocation is worthless to them, and refusing to show any leg on allocation after flagging it as 'genuinely open' in Round 1 would read as bad faith and accelerate the Japan/Korea joint dispute dynamic; (b) table the full authorised package (1.5Mt/900kt) — rejected because Brussels explicitly forbade approaching ceilings before Round 3 and because gifting allocation plus volume in one step leaves nothing to trade for the disapplication modification and the reciprocal track. Anchoring at 1Mt/600kt does three things: it demonstrates the allocation concession is real (concrete figures, not adjectives), it leaves two full rounds of volume headroom to spend against the disapplication and EU exporters' UK quotas, and it makes the tranche/disapplication substitution explicit exactly as Brussels instructed. Holding 50% OQR preserves the late-round concession. Offering the review clause unconditionally is cheap, complies with the instruction that it 'may be offered', and gives my counterpart something deliverable to London this round, which sustains momentum toward June and reduces the temptation to coordinate with Japan and Korea.

public_message: Thank you — that was a substantive response, and I want to acknowledge it properly before addressing what remains between us. First, the Union's movement to country-specific allocation anchored in historic trade, administered by licensing, is significant, and I will report it to London as such. The UK welcomes it. It answers the core structural objection we raised in Round 1, and it gives this negotiation a shape it did not have when we sat down. Second, the unconditional offer of a mandatory review clause and a four-to-five-year duration is noted and accepted as common ground — let us treat duration and review as settled elements of the architecture, and I would propose four years with a mandatory review at the midpoint, which gives both our industries predictability without pretending the measure is permanent. Third, I take careful note of your formulation on the disapplication provision: modified application, within a balanced package, if the rest of the package moves. I will report that precisely. For the record, the UK's legal position is unchanged: disapplication of FTA tariff reductions sits in obvious tension with the Union's TCA obligations, and we are taking soundings on that question. But I hear the distinction you have drawn between the provision as notified and its treatment of TCA partners, and I am prepared to explore what 'modified application' means in practice — once I know what volume it trades against. Which brings me to volume. You have asked the UK to move its tranche figure, and you have characterised your own thinking as directional. I must be equally direct: the UK moved first in this negotiation by tabling concrete numbers. It is now for the Union to put a number on the table — a total pool and a UK tranche — that the Trade Policy Committee could actually consider. I cannot negotiate against an adjective. You have said the distance is very large; then show me the Union's end of it, and I will show you whether the UK can close it. Until there is an EU figure on paper, the UK's ask stands: a total pool of 2.5 million tonnes with a UK tranche of 2 million tonnes, an out-of-quota bound rate of 25%, licensing administration tied to a historic reference period, four years with mandatory review, and carve-outs on the lines I am about to hand across. On administration, since you have met us on licensing, I will say this: our strong preference is licensing anchored in a historic reference period, but if the Union has domestic reasons to need a hybrid model or a modified design, that is a conversation I am authorised to have — against movement on volume. On carve-outs, I am tabling a line-by-line paper identifying the specific tariff lines where UK supply is concentrated and EU domestic production is limited or absent. On those lines, the modification imposes real costs on EU downstream users for no protective benefit, and carving them out costs the Council nothing. I would ask for the Union's engagement on that paper line by line, as the earliest concrete deliverable of this negotiation. On melt-and-pour: accepted as architecture, not conceded as a favour — the UK has no difficulty with genuine origin discipline, as our own measure demonstrates. Finally, reciprocity. I hear clearly that preservation of EU country-specific allocations under the UK's steel measure is a formal objective on the same footing as our tranche. The UK is prepared to explore coherence between the two regimes in principle, and I say that warmly and sincerely. But coherence is a two-way structure: it cannot be built with one side's contribution. Any concrete discussion of EU allocations under our measure can only follow, not precede, the Union tabling its volume figures. That is sequencing, not refusal. So to summarise where the UK stands at the close of Round 2: allocation and administration — converging. Duration and review — settled. Disapplication — door open, price unknown. Volume — the Union must now name its number. Carve-outs — paper tabled, engagement requested. Reciprocity — in principle, in sequence. I look forward to the Union's figures.

report: The EU made its first substantial movement but still has not tabled volume figures. It formally moved from global first-come first-served allocation to country-specific allocation anchored in historic trade, administered by licensing, while describing this as its most significant available concession and explicitly linking it to movement on volume, FTA disapplication and reciprocal treatment under the UK's steel measure. It also offered a mandatory review clause and a four-to-five-year duration unconditionally, while maintaining melt-and-pour origin rules as part of the regime architecture. On the FTA disapplication provision, the EU did not withdraw it, but stated for the first time that 'modified application' for TCA partners could be discussed within a balanced package if the rest of the package moves. The EU rejected our proposed UK tranche of 2 million tonnes within a 2.5 million tonne pool as negating the modification, but indicated only directional scope for a substantially enlarged total pool and a meaningful UK tranche. I acknowledged the significance of its movement on allocation and licensing, treated duration and review as broad common ground while proposing four years with a midpoint review, accepted melt-and-pour as legitimate architecture, and tabled our line-by-line carve-out paper. I declined to move on volume before the EU tables concrete total-pool and UK-tranche figures, reiterated that any reciprocity discussion must follow those figures, and preserved our legal position on TCA inconsistency without escalating. The current state is therefore: allocation and administration substantially converged; duration and review close but not finally settled; carve-outs under consideration; disapplication potentially negotiable in modified form; volume and out-of-quota rate still unresolved; reciprocity acknowledged in principle but not yet substantively traded.

instruction: Strong round — you consolidated the EU's movement on allocation and licensing without conceding a single number, and you forced the burden of tabling figures onto them. That is exactly where we want to be. For Round 3, your objectives in order: (1) Lock in the gains. Open by proposing that the agreed elements be recorded as settled architecture: country-specific allocation anchored in historic trade, licensing administration, four-year duration with mandatory midpoint review, melt-and-pour origin discipline. Get the EU to confirm these are no longer in play — this protects them if volume talks get rough. (2) Volume. The EU has said it will table figures. When it does, do not accept or reject at the table, but you may now respond with staged movement per the authority below — do NOT jump to your floor in one move. If the EU's opening number is derisory (a UK tranche below 600,000t), say so plainly and hold at 2Mt; derisory openings must be named as such or they anchor the endgame. (3) Out-of-quota rate. If the EU tables volume, insist it also tables a rate — do not let them settle volume while leaving 50% untouched. Signal that rate relief and volume are both components of the compensation and the UK will assess the package as a whole. (4) Disapplication. Ask the EU to define 'modified application' concretely and in writing: does it mean within-quota TCA treatment preserved for UK-origin steel? A UK-specific exemption from the provision? Do not indicate any formulation is acceptable; say you will report it. (5) Reciprocity. If the EU tables credible volume figures, you may — for the first time — acknowledge that preservation of EU exporters' existing country-specific allocations under our steel measure is something the UK could look at constructively as part of a final package. Preservation only. No uplift, no percentages, no tonnages. Frame it as a signal of seriousness unlocked by their movement, sequenced to a final package. (6) Carve-outs. Press for a technical session on your line-by-line paper before Round 4 and ask the EU to indicate which lines it can carve out. If the EU engages seriously, you may indicate that agreed carve-outs on the priority lines would be factored into London's assessment of the overall volume package — but give no conversion rate at the table. (7) TCA legal point: do not repeat the challenge this round unless provoked — you have made the record; let Japan and Korea carry that argument for now.

authority.notes: Staged volume plan — each step is strictly conditional and you should not expect to use all of it in Round 3: STEP 1 — you may move from 2.0Mt to 1.75Mt only if the EU has tabled a total pool of at least 2.0Mt, a UK tranche of at least 1.2Mt, and an out-of-quota rate at or below 35%. STEP 2 — you may move to 1.5Mt only if the EU improves to a tranche of at least 1.4Mt, a rate at or below 30%, commits to carve-outs on at least half our priority lines, and tables a written formulation of 'modified application' that preserves zero-duty TCA treatment within the UK tranche. STEP 3 — movement below 1.5Mt toward the 1.2Mt floor is RESERVED for Round 4 and a final package only, and requires: tranche confirmed at that level with licensing, out-of-quota rate at or below 25%, all priority carve-outs, modified application preserving TCA treatment in-quota, and the reciprocity coin described below. Do not go below 1.2Mt under any circumstances — below that figure the deal cannot be defended to ministers or the industry and we are better off taking the retaliation track. RECIPROCITY: preservation of existing EU country-specific allocations under our safeguard is your first and preferred coin — you may signal constructiveness on it this round as instructed, but formal offer of preservation only against a tranche of at least 1.4Mt. Any uplift above preservation remains capped at 15% of current EU allocations, is reserved for Round 4, and remains conditional on country-specific allocation plus a UK tranche of at least 1.5Mt. RATE-VOLUME TRADEOFF: volume is worth more to us than rate — ministers are judged on plant survival, which is volume-driven. As a rough internal guide, treat each 100,000t of tranche as worth roughly 5 percentage points of out-of-quota rate; do not trade tranche tonnage for rate relief at worse than that ratio, and never below the 1.2Mt floor at any rate. DISAPPLICATION: acceptable end-states, in descending order: (a) UK-specific exemption from the provision; (b) disapplication applying only to out-of-quota trade, preserving zero-duty TCA treatment within the UK tranche; (c) any other formulation with equivalent commercial effect. Nothing short of equivalent effect is acceptable, and you must not signal that any of these is acceptable — your line remains that the provision as notified is legally untenable and we are evaluating their formulation. CARVE-OUTS: treat agreed carve-outs on priority lines as worth up to roughly 250,000t of tranche volume in your overall assessment, but do not reveal this conversion at the table. JAPAN/KOREA: holding line only — 'the UK is taking soundings and keeping all options under review; our present focus is the bilateral track.' No coordination, no joint language, no visible escalation this round.

response_to_requests.request: Detailed authority for reciprocity under the UK's steel measure, including whether preservation of existing EU allocations can be offered before any uplift.

private_rationale: Round 2 went better than expected — the EU conceded our core structural demand (country-specific allocation plus licensing) in only the second round, which tells me their mandate is under pressure from steel-consuming member states and the June deadline is biting them harder than us. The risk now is twofold: (1) the EU tables a lowball tranche (400-800kt) dressed up as 'substantially enlarged' to anchor the endgame, and (2) our own side panics and takes a thin deal because ministers are frightened of the two plant closures. The staged plan is designed to prevent both: it keeps us at 2Mt against derisory openings while giving Geneva enough room to keep momentum against credible ones. My honest assessment of the landing zone is 1.4-1.6Mt UK tranche, ~28-30% out-of-quota, licensing, 4 years with review, in-quota TCA preservation, half our carve-outs, plus preservation of EU allocations under our safeguard. That package is sellable: it covers the majority of historic trade at zero or low duty and gives the Minister something to take to the plant owners alongside the subsidy track. I am keeping Step 3 and the 15% uplift in reserve because Round 4 is where the EU's June deadline gives us maximum leverage — they cannot afford to go back to Council empty-handed, and a no-deal leaves them facing simultaneous retaliation threats from us, Turkey, Korea, India and Japan. The FTA disapplication is my biggest quiet asset: the EU has already signalled it is movable, and every tonne I extract for it is invisible to the other claimants. I have not told Geneva that 1.2Mt would in fact be accepted in extremis with the full package — they negotiate better believing the floor is firmer than it is — but the instruction as written protects the floor anyway. If Round 3 ends with EU figures above 1.2Mt tranche and a rate below 35%, we are on track to settle in Round 4 at or above the defensible line.

reasoning: There are no agreed terms on the table to accept. Genuine convergence was achieved in Round 2 on allocation method (country-specific, licensing), and duration/review is effectively settled at 4 years with a midpoint review, but volume, the disapplication, reciprocity and the out-of-quota rate all remain open. Accepting the UK's current position would negate the modification itself. Accepting the default now would forfeit a negotiation that is moving in our direction: the UK has shown real engagement, the disapplication trade-off structure (in-quota TCA treatment vs. larger tranche) is a strong lever, and the reciprocity track on EU exporters' UK quotas is alive. The June deadline pressures both sides, and the UK's no-deal exposure is worse than ours. Round 3 should open at 1.15Mt total with a 650-700kt UK tranche, moving to the 1.25Mt/750kt ceiling only on demonstrated UK movement, with the 1.5Mt/900kt envelope and any movement toward 40% reserved for a single final Round 4 package conditional on preserved EU country-specific shares under the UK measure, the approved disapplication formula, melt-and-pour rules, and limited carve-outs.

There is no complete package on the table to accept: the EU has not yet tabled any volume figures (total pool or UK tranche) or moved on the out-of-quota rate, and the 'modified application' formulation on FTA disapplication remains undefined. Equally, letting the process lapse would forfeit real, hard-won movement: the EU has formally conceded country-specific allocation anchored in historic trade with licensing administration, offered unconditional review and four-to-five-year duration, and opened a conditional door on TCA treatment — all of which address our core structural objections. Round 3 strategy per London's instructions: lock in the settled architecture, force the EU to table concrete volume and rate figures, name any derisory opening as such, hold at the 2Mt ask pending their numbers, and release staged movement (2.0Mt toward 1.75Mt, then 1.5Mt) only against the defined conditional packages. public_message: Thank you. The UK asked the Union to name its number, and the Union will now do so. I am authorised to table the following, and I want to be precise about its status: these are concrete figures that the Trade Policy Committee could genuinely consider, presented as elements of a single conditional package, not as standalone concessions. First, volume: a total pool of 1.15 million tonnes per year, within which a UK country-specific tranche of 675,000 tonnes, administered by licensing anchored in a historic reference period. That is nearly three times the notified pool, and a UK tranche larger than the entire original quota — I would ask London to weigh it in those terms, and against what the absence of any agreement delivers: 400,000 tonnes, global, first-come first-served. Second, the disapplication provision, on which I can now offer a defined formulation. For TCA partners, preferential tariff treatment would be preserved for trade within the country-specific tranche; the disapplication provision would apply only to out-of-quota trade, where the bound rate applies. In practical terms, UK-origin steel within your tranche enters on TCA terms. I would ask the UK to consider that this answers the substance of the concern you have raised — and I say so conscious that the concern is not yours alone. Third, let me make the structure of the remaining negotiation explicit, because I believe it helps both of us. Tranche volume and the disapplication trade against each other: the package I have described pairs the negotiated tranche with TCA treatment preserved in-quota. A materially larger tranche would require the provision to apply as notified. The UK cannot maximise both, and the sooner we agree which axis matters more to London, the sooner we close. Fourth, on your carve-out paper: we have completed an initial technical read. There are a small number of lines — I would say up to three or four — where EU production is genuinely minimal and where we see scope to agree carve-outs, but only within the final package, not as a standalone deliverable. I propose our technical teams meet this week to identify them. Fifth, reciprocity. You described your position as sequencing, not refusal. I accept that, and I would observe that it cuts both ways: the figures I have just tabled are sequenced too. Their confirmation depends on concrete UK commitment to preserve EU exporters' existing country-specific quota shares under your own steel measure. That is a formal objective on the same footing as your tranche, and it cannot remain a principle while my figures become facts. Finally, for the record: four years with a mandatory midpoint review is agreed as settled; melt-and-pour origin rules stand as architecture; the out-of-quota bound rate remains 50% as tabled. So the Union has now named its number, named its formulation, and named its structure. I look forward to the UK's movement.

public_message: Thank you. The Union has now named its number, and I want to acknowledge what that represents: a total pool nearly three times the notified quota, a UK-specific tranche, a defined formulation on the disapplication provision, and a commitment to technical work on carve-outs. Round 2 gave this negotiation structure; Round 3 has given it content. I will report it to London in those terms. Let me respond in the same structured way. First, settled architecture. The UK proposes that we now record as no longer in play: country-specific allocation anchored in historic trade; licensing administration tied to a historic reference period; four-year duration with a mandatory midpoint review, as you confirmed; and melt-and-pour origin discipline. I ask the Union to confirm these are settled, so neither side re-opens them if the volume discussion becomes difficult. Second, volume. You ask London to weigh 675,000 tonnes against the notified pool. London will weigh it against a different baseline: 2.4 million tonnes of average annual UK exports. On that baseline the tranche tabled covers barely a quarter of historic trade, and the entire pool would not cover UK trade alone. And I put to the Union a problem of its own arithmetic: Turkey and Korea each ship larger volumes to the EU than the UK does, and India and Japan have reserved rights. A pool of 1.15 million tonnes cannot deliver substantially equivalent compensation to five members whose combined historic trade is a multiple of that figure. The pool must be defensible across the whole Article XXVIII process, not merely between us — and at 1.15 million it is not. The UK does not treat the figure as derisory; it is a genuine number and I say so. But it is not a number on which this negotiation can close. Our ask stands: a 2.5 million tonne pool and a 2 million tonne UK tranche. The Union knows the distance, and I look to Round 4 for its further movement. Third, the out-of-quota rate. I note the Union's position that 50% remains as tabled, and I must be plain: that cannot be the end of the matter. A 50% bound rate atop a constrained tranche converts residual historic trade into prohibited trade. Rate relief is a component of the compensation, and the UK will assess the package as a whole — tranche, rate, carve-outs and the disapplication formulation together. I ask the Union to come to Round 4 with movement on the rate as well as on volume. Fourth, the disapplication formulation. I will report it precisely: preferential treatment preserved for TCA partners' trade within country-specific tranches, the provision applying to out-of-quota trade. I ask for it in writing, and I have technical questions — how it interacts with licence administration, whether it attaches to origin or to the partner, and how it operates where a tranche is under-filled. The UK's position on the provision as notified is unchanged and a matter of record. On the structure you described — that a materially larger tranche requires the provision as notified — I observe, purely as a matter of logic, that the Union's own formulation dissolves that linkage: if TCA treatment applies to in-quota trade whatever the tranche's size, then enlarging the tranche simply enlarges the quantity entering on TCA terms; it does not require the provision as notified. The tradeoff you describe is one of volume, not of legal architecture — and volume is exactly where we remain apart. Fifth, reciprocity. The Union has now put figures on the table, and in response I can say the following, choosing my words carefully: preservation of EU exporters' existing country-specific quota allocations under the UK's steel measure is something the UK could look at constructively as part of a final package. That is a signal of seriousness, unlocked by the Union's movement today, and it is sequenced to a final package. It is preservation I am describing — I am not in a position to go further, and I would not want the Union to read more into the sentence than it contains. Sixth, carve-outs. We welcome the technical read and accept the proposed session this week. The UK will come with its priority lines identified; we ask the Union to come prepared to name the lines it can carve out. As I have said, agreed carve-outs on our priority lines will be factored into London's assessment of the overall volume package — I cannot offer a conversion rate, but the Union should understand that progress on the paper moves the negotiation as a whole. To close: the elements are now all on the table. Allocation and administration — settled. Duration and review — settled. Disapplication — a formulation tabled and under evaluation. Carve-outs — a technical session agreed. Reciprocity — constructively acknowledged, in sequence. What remains is the heart of it: a tranche and a rate that together preserve a viable UK industry. The Union has moved once on architecture and once on numbers. Round 4 must be the round in which the numbers become a landing zone.
