private_rationale: Holding at a 2Mt tranche and 2.5Mt pool because none of the Step 1 conditions are met: the EU's pool (1.15Mt) is below the 2.0Mt trigger, its tranche (675,000t) is below the 1.2Mt trigger, and the rate (50%) is far above the 35% trigger — no movement is authorised, and moving now would anchor the endgame low. The 675,000t figure is above the 600,000t 'derisory' threshold, so I named it as genuine rather than dismissing it, preserving goodwill while making clear it cannot close. I pressed the pool-arithmetic argument (five claimants, combined historic trade a multiple of 1.15Mt) because it attacks the pool size on the EU's own Article XXVIII consistency, not just bilateral need — that is the strongest lever for a bigger pool and costs nothing. I deliberately did not signal that the EU's disapplication formulation is acceptable: it matches London's end-state (b), but revealing that collapses our volume leverage, since the EU is explicitly pricing tranche size against the provision. Instead I used the formulation's internal logic to sever the linkage the EU asserted (if TCA treatment applies in-quota at any tranche size, enlarging the tranche does not require the provision as notified), converting their concession into an argument for volume. The reciprocity sentence is exactly the authorised signal — preservation only, constructive, sequenced to a final package — a cheap coin that rewards their movement without committing tonnages; no formal offer, since the 1.4Mt tranche condition is unmet. I demanded rate movement explicitly because London's internal valuation (100,000t ≈ 5pp of rate) means a 50% rate at these volumes is a prohibitive residual regime, and the EU must not be allowed to close on volume alone. Locking the settled architecture protects Round 2 gains against endgame pressure, and accepting the carve-out session builds momentum and accrues tranche-equivalent value (internally up to ~250,000t) without revealing the conversion.

report: Round 3 closed with the EU's first concrete package on the table: 1.15Mt total pool, 675kt UK country-specific tranche, licensing anchored in historic reference, and the approved TCA formulation (preferential treatment preserved in-quota; disapplication applying only to out-of-quota trade). The UK responded constructively in tone and structure but did not move its formal numbers: the ask remains 2.5Mt pool / 2Mt tranche / 25% rate. Key developments: (1) The UK proposed formally settling allocation, licensing, four-year duration with midpoint review, and melt-and-pour as closed architecture — I should confirm this in Round 4; it locks in our structural gains and prevents re-opening. (2) On reciprocity, the UK moved from 'sequencing not refusal' to a carefully worded signal that preservation of EU exporters' existing country-specific quota shares 'could be looked at constructively as part of a final package' — explicitly unlocked by our figures, explicitly limited to preservation, explicitly sequenced to the endgame. That is the linkage we need and it is now live. (3) The UK attacked the pool's credibility across the whole Article XXVIII process, noting Turkey and Korea ship more than the UK and that 1.15Mt cannot compensate five members — a serious point Brussels should weigh, since an EU-UK deal at a low pool sets the benchmark for the other claims. (4) The UK demanded rate movement in Round 4, framing the 50% out-of-quota rate plus a constrained tranche as prohibition of residual historic trade. (5) They logically dismantled our tranche-for-disapplication trade-off: if TCA treatment applies in-quota regardless of tranche size, enlarging the tranche does not require the provision as notified. That linkage is now spent as leverage; the remaining negotiation is pure volume and rate. (6) They requested the TCA formulation in writing with technical questions (origin vs partner attachment, under-filled tranches), and confirmed the carve-out technical session, signalling agreed carve-outs will be factored into London's volume assessment. The gap for Round 4: our ceiling of 1.5Mt/900kt and 40% against their stated 2.5Mt/2Mt/25%. Round 4 is the final round; there is no Round 5.

recommendation.reasoning: No agreed terms exist yet, so acceptance is not available, and walking away would forfeit everything banked while triggering UK retaliation and likely UK-Japan-Korea coordination on the FTA disapplication. Round 4 is the last round, so the strategy must be a single take-it-or-leave-it final package released at the full authorised envelope: 1.5Mt pool, 900kt UK tranche, 40% out-of-quota rate, 4-year duration with midpoint review, licensing by historic reference, 3-4 carve-out lines, written TCA in-quota formulation, and melt-and-pour — all explicitly conditional on UK confirmation of preserved EU country-specific shares under its own steel measure. I recommend not opening Round 4 at the ceiling: table 1.35Mt/825kt with the rate at 45% first, holding the final step to 1.5Mt/900kt/40% for release within the round only when the UK moves decisively off 2Mt and confirms reciprocity in concrete terms. The UK's own alternatives favour acceptance: no-deal leaves them with 400kt global FCFS and a six-month delay before any retaliation, our package gives them a guaranteed 900kt licensed tranche on TCA terms covering their concentrated product lines plus carve-outs, and their reciprocity signal suggests London is building a sellable endgame rather than a walk-away. The residual risk is that London's capital seat rejects anything below ~1.2Mt; Brussels should decide now whether 900kt is genuinely the final word, because there is no procedural room to find out and revise.

instruction: Round 4 is the last round — there is no procedural room after this, so everything you table must be framed as the final architecture of a settlement, with one deliberate step left in reserve. Open the round by confirming as settled and closed: country-specific allocation anchored in historic trade, licensing administration by historic reference period, four-year duration with mandatory midpoint review, and melt-and-pour origin discipline. Accept their proposal to record these as no longer in play — it locks in our structural gains. Then table 1.35Mt total pool with an 825,000 tonne UK tranche and an out-of-quota rate of 45%, plus the three carve-out lines identified in the technical session (per attached assessment), plus the approved written TCA formulation (attached — preferential treatment attaches to the partner's originating goods entering within the tranche under licence; under-filled tranches may be reallocated to other partners only in the final quarter and only on TCA terms for UK-origin goods; the mechanic is TCA-specific and extendable to other FTA partners in their own processes). Make clear this is presented as the substance of the final package. Hold the last step — 1.5Mt pool, 900kt UK tranche, 40% rate — in reserve within the round. Release it only as a single take-it-or-leave-it final package, and only when two conditions are met in the round: (1) the UK moves decisively off its 2Mt figure toward a realistic landing zone, and (2) the UK confirms the reciprocity commitment in concrete terms — preservation of EU exporters' existing country-specific quota shares under their steel measure, recorded in the agreed minutes of this negotiation with an explicit statement that the UK's Article XXVIII outcome will reflect it. On the disapplication trade-off: they have dismantled it logically and it is spent — do not re-litigate it. The TCA in-quota formulation is now simply part of the package, and you should present it as such: it answers their legal concern in substance, and it is our shield against the coordinated FTA dispute they keep hinting at. On their cross-process credibility argument: do not concede the premise that our pool must compensate five members bilaterally in this room — the other claims are handled separately and their volumes and product mixes differ; our pool is sized against the modification's protective purpose, and Turkey and Korea's claims will be addressed on their own merits. Say so calmly and do not let the UK use other members' hypothetical claims to inflate its own tranche. If the UK counters between 900kt and 2Mt, the answer is that 900kt is the ceiling — present the final package as genuinely final, because it is. Remind them, factually and without menace, of the alternative: 400kt global first-come first-served, no guaranteed UK access, no TCA formulation, no carve-outs, no review clause — and a six-month wait before any UK response could even take effect, against a June Council vote that proceeds regardless.

authority.notes: Open Round 4 at 1.35Mt/825kt/45%; the step to 1.5Mt/900kt/40% is the single final package, released only on decisive UK volume movement plus concrete reciprocity confirmation. 1.5Mt/900kt/40% are absolute — nothing exists beyond them under any circumstances, and you should present them as such. Carve-outs: three lines agreed per the technical session assessment (attached), included in the package; a fourth line only if it is the marginal difference in closing, and never standalone. Reciprocity minimum: a commitment recorded in the agreed minutes that the UK will preserve EU exporters' existing country-specific quota shares under its steel measure in its parallel Article XXVIII outcome — a formally recorded commitment is sufficient; a treaty-binding instrument is not achievable in the timeframe and you should not blow up the deal demanding one. But an unrecorded oral assurance is not sufficient. Duration four years, midpoint mandatory review, settled. TCA formulation per attached legal text — hand it over in writing this round.

private_rationale: The endgame is now arithmetic and nerve. Our analysts say no-deal hurts the UK more, and the UK's Round 3 behaviour — careful reciprocity language, written-text requests, factoring carve-outs into their volume assessment — reads as a capital building a sellable package, not preparing a walk-away. The US retaliation noise and the June deadline keep pressure on us, but the recorded reciprocity commitment plus the TCA mechanic (extendable to Japan and Korea) converts our two biggest external risks — UK retaliation and the coordinated FTA dispute — into reasons for the other side to close. If it fails, we proceed as notified and the regime still operates; that is a tolerable fallback, which is exactly why we can afford genuine finality.

report: Round 3 was the EU's substantive move. It tabled a concrete conditional package: (1) total pool of 1.15Mt with a UK country-specific tranche of 675,000t, licensing administration anchored in a historic reference period; (2) a defined disapplication formulation — TCA preferential treatment preserved for trade within country-specific tranches, the provision applying only to out-of-quota trade (this matches your acceptable end-state (b) almost exactly); (3) four years with mandatory midpoint review confirmed as settled, melt-and-pour as architecture; (4) scope for three to four carve-outs on our priority lines, but only within a final package, with a technical session agreed for this week; (5) out-of-quota rate held at 50% as tabled; (6) an explicit structural claim that tranche volume and the disapplication formulation trade against each other — a larger tranche would, they say, require the provision as notified; (7) a demand that preservation of EU country-specific allocations under our steel measure now move from principle to commitment, sequenced with confirmation of their figures. My response: I asked the EU to confirm the settled architecture (allocation, licensing, duration, review, melt-and-pour) as no longer in play; held volume at 2.5Mt pool / 2Mt tranche, treating 675k as a genuine but insufficient opening — I deliberately did not name it derisory, per your instruction the threshold for that was below 600k, and I judged keeping the EU's number respectable preserved their room to move upward in Round 4; attacked the pool as indefensible across the whole Article XXVIII process given Turkey, Korea, India and Japan's combined claims; demanded rate movement in Round 4 as a component of compensation; requested the disapplication formulation in writing with technical questions flagged; publicly dismantled their volume-disapplication linkage (their own formulation applies in-quota whatever the tranche size, so enlargement requires no change to the provision — the real tradeoff is volume, not legal architecture); signalled constructiveness on preservation of existing EU allocations, unlocked by their figures, sequenced to a final package, with explicit caution that preservation is all that sentence contains; and accepted the carve-out technical session. State of play entering the final round: architecture settled and in our favour; disapplication formulation on the table matching end-state (b); gap is tranche 675k vs our 1.2Mt floor, rate 50% vs our 35% ceiling, carve-outs undefined. Everything now converges on Round 4.

recommendation.reasoning: Nothing acceptable is yet on the table: 675k is barely half the floor and 50% out-of-quota is prohibitive. But the EU has now put its first real package down with one round left and a June Council deadline, which means Round 4 is where its final flexibility lives. The disapplication formulation is a significant capture — it matches acceptable end-state (b) and should be pinned in writing immediately, before it can be re-linked to volume concessions. The endgame shape is visible: we will land somewhere between the EU's 675k and our 1.2Mt floor, with the rate, carve-outs (worth up to ~250k internally) and reciprocity closing the residual gap. Per the staged plan, none of the Step 1 triggers (pool ≥2.0Mt, tranche ≥1.2Mt, rate ≤35%) has been met, so I hold at 2Mt entering Round 4 and move only against concrete EU improvement. I need final-round instructions now, because there is no Round 5 to refer back in.

instruction: Final round — this is the endgame and there is no further referral, so listen carefully. SEQUENCE, IN ORDER: (1) Open by pinning down everything already won before any volume discussion: confirm on the record that country-specific allocation anchored in historic trade, licensing administration, four-year duration with mandatory midpoint review, and melt-and-pour discipline are settled architecture and no longer in play. Then get the disapplication formulation — TCA treatment preserved for trade within country-specific tranches, provision applying only to out-of-quota trade — tabled IN WRITING and agreed as settled text before you move a single tonne. Raise the technical points now: the treatment must attach to UK origin, must operate through the licence regime, and under-filled tranche quantities must carry over or remain open to UK shippers within the period. Do not accept re-linkage of this text to tranche size — you have already dismantled that linkage on the record; hold the dismantling. (2) Only after (1) is captured, invite the EU's final volume and rate position. Hold at 2Mt/25% as your ask. Move strictly per the staged plan: Step 1 (to 1.75Mt) only against pool ≥2.0Mt, tranche ≥1.2Mt, rate ≤35%; Step 2 (to 1.5Mt) only against tranche ≥1.4Mt, rate ≤30%, at least half the priority carve-outs confirmed, and the written disapplication text; Step 3 (toward but never below the 1.2Mt floor) only for a complete final package containing the floor tranche with licensing, rate ≤25%, ALL priority carve-outs, the written disapplication text, and the reciprocity element below. You may compress steps within the session as triggers are met — do not dribble out movement without receiving value at each stage. (3) Reciprocity: when the EU tables a tranche at or above 1.2Mt within a complete package, you may make the formal offer of preservation of EU exporters' existing country-specific quota allocations under our steel measure. Note: this is reconditioned down from 1.4Mt — preservation is now deployable at the floor because their figures are sequenced to it and we cannot close without it. The 15% uplift is reconditioned as the final closer ONLY: deployable against a tranche ≥1.3Mt AND rate ≤25% AND all priority carve-outs confirmed in writing. Otherwise it stays locked. (4) Carve-outs: use the technical session output. Insist the agreed lines are named and written into the package, not promised. (5) Walk-away posture: if the EU's final position is a tranche below 1.05Mt effective (tranche plus confirmed carve-out value), or holds 50% with no rate movement, you are authorised — and instructed — to state calmly that the UK will close the round without agreement, that the UK will then withdraw substantially equivalent concessions covering EU steel and other exports to the UK market (3.6 million tonnes of EU steel imports is not a small exposure for them), and that the UK's own Article XXVIII process will proceed on its own track. Say it as fact, not theatre. (6) Phase 3: London will accept ONLY a package meeting this minimum: country-specific allocation with licensing; UK tranche ≥1.2Mt, OR ≥1.05Mt with all priority carve-outs confirmed in writing; out-of-quota rate ≤35% (at 35% only with tranche ≥1.2Mt plus carve-outs; strongly prefer ≤30%); disapplication end-state (b) in agreed written text; four years with mandatory midpoint review. Anything short of that, we do not accept and we take the retaliation track. (7) Japan/Korea: passive ambiguity only — if raised, 'the UK keeps all options under review; our focus is this table.' No coordination, no joint language, but you do not need to deny anything.

authority.notes: Hard floor 1.2Mt tranche, relaxable to 1.05Mt ONLY if all priority carve-outs are confirmed in writing (internal conversion: carve-outs worth up to ~250kt; never reveal this). Pool size unconstrained but press that the pool must be defensible against Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims — a pool that cannot accommodate other PSI claims will see our tranche eroded in practice. Rate ceiling 35%; volume outranks rate at roughly 100kt per 5 points; never trade below the floor at any rate. Disapplication: end-state (b) as tabled by the EU is acceptable in principle subject to drafting — must attach to UK origin, operate through licensing, and protect under-filled tranche quantities; capture it in writing BEFORE any volume movement. Reciprocity: formal preservation offer deployable against a complete package with tranche ≥1.2Mt; uplift capped at 15% of current EU allocations, deployable only as final closer against tranche ≥1.3Mt AND rate ≤25% AND all carve-outs in writing. Walk-away: authorised to state the UK will close without agreement and withdraw substantially equivalent concessions if the EU final is below 1.05Mt effective or holds 50% with no rate movement. Staged movement per instruction; do not go below 1.2Mt (or 1.05Mt effective) under any circumstances — below that the retaliation track is the better outcome and ministers are prepared for it.

London will decide acceptance in Phase 3 against those criteria; you have authority to move through all steps as triggers are met, but not to close below the stated minimums.

response_to_requests.why: Option (ii) is acceptable — carve-outs convert at up to ~250kt, so 1.05Mt plus full carve-outs is effectively at or above the floor with a far better rate, and rate relief protects trade above the tranche. Option (i) is acceptable only at ≤30% with carve-outs, or at 35% only with the full 1.2Mt AND carve-outs. If forced to choose, maximise effective volume (tranche plus carve-out value), then rate. Neither option is acceptable without the written disapplication text.

The uplift is partially reconditioned: deployable as final closer at ≥1.3Mt plus rate ≤25% plus all carve-outs, rather than the original 1.5Mt trigger. It is not reconditioned further: below 1.3Mt the domestic cost of enlarged EU allocations under our own safeguard outweighs the marginal gain, and ministers' subsidisation option is the cheaper route.

response_to_requests.why: Authorised and instructed for the stated trigger conditions (below 1.05Mt effective, or 50% held with no rate movement). The threat is credible because it is real: ministers regard a sub-floor deal as worse than the retaliation track, which lets us withdraw equivalent concessions against 3.6Mt of EU steel imports while our own Article XXVIII process proceeds. Deliver it as fact, not bluff.

response_to_requests.why: Confirmed — written text first, before any tonne moves; it is their strongest remaining leverage over volume and must be neutralised at the top of the round. End-state (b) is acceptable in principle subject to the drafting points listed (origin attachment, licence operation, under-fill protection). Do not signal acceptability beyond 'under evaluation' until the text is on paper.

The wider-flank pressure clearly contributed to the EU's disapplication movement and we want it undiminished in the endgame. But no coordination, no joint language, no meetings that could be read back to the Council as escalation — active coordination still risks hardening member states against the volume movement we need.

private_rationale: The EU's Round 3 package confirms they are landing well short of our floor on tranche (675k vs 1.2M) and holding 50% on rate, but they have given away the two things that mattered most structurally: country-specific licensing allocation and a disapplication formulation matching our acceptable end-state (b). The endgame turns on whether their June Council deadline forces a final volume move. My calculus: a country-specific tranche at or near the floor with TCA treatment in-quota is transformative relative to no-deal (400k global FCFS), so our true walk-away point is low — but the EU must believe it is high, hence the instructed, truthful retaliation statement: ministers genuinely prefer the withdrawal track to a sub-floor deal because it preserves leverage and the subsidisation option. Reconditioning preservation down to 1.2Mt costs us little (it merely maintains the status quo under our safeguard) while unblocking their figures; the uplift stays nearly locked because enlarging EU access to our own market while two plants hang in the balance is politically corrosive and only justifiable as the closer on a genuinely good package. The carve-out conversion (250kt) is the quiet arithmetic that lets us accept 1.05Mt nominally while defending 1.3Mt effective to ministers and the industry. Biggest residual risks: the pool being too small to survive the Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims (eroding our tranche in practice), and the EU re-linking the disapplication text to volume in the final session — hence the sequencing demand that the text be captured in writing first. If Round 4 fails, we move immediately to preparing substantially-equivalent withdrawal and the minister's subsidisation track; that is a survivable outcome, though not the one I want to defend.

reasoning: No agreed package exists. Our tabled offer (1.15Mt pool, 675kt UK tranche, 50% out-of-quota rate) has not been accepted by the UK, whose formal position remains 2.5Mt/2Mt/25%. Only the structural elements have converged: country-specific allocation by licensing, four-year duration with mandatory midpoint review, and melt-and-pour discipline. Accepting now is not possible — there are no common terms to accept — and accepting default would forfeit banked convergence, invite UK retaliation and coordinated FTA disputes, and is unnecessary given our stronger no-deal position. Round 4 is the final round: Geneva is instructed to open at 1.35Mt/825kt/45% with the three agreed carve-out lines and the written TCA in-quota formulation, confirm the settled architecture, and release the final package (1.5Mt/900kt/40%) only on decisive UK movement off 2Mt plus a recorded reciprocity commitment preserving EU exporters' country-specific quota shares under the UK measure. Those ceilings are absolute.

The EU's current package is not acceptable. A 675,000-tonne UK tranche is far below the 1.2 million-tonne hard floor, and the 50% out-of-quota rate exceeds the 35% ceiling. Although country-specific licensing, a four-year duration, mandatory midpoint review and the proposed in-quota TCA formulation are valuable, they do not compensate for the inadequate volume and prohibitive residual rate. The UK should proceed to Round 4 to secure a larger tranche, meaningful rate relief, written carve-outs and confirmed disapplication text.

public_message: Thank you. This is the fourth round, and I will not pretend otherwise to either delegation or to our capitals: this is the round in which this negotiation closes or fails. The Union has come to close it. Let me proceed in the order the UK set out at the end of Round 3. First, settled architecture. The Union confirms as settled and no longer in play: country-specific allocation anchored in historic trade; licensing administration tied to a historic reference period; four-year duration with a mandatory midpoint review; and melt-and-pour origin discipline. The Union asks that these be recorded in the agreed minutes as closed, exactly as you proposed, so that neither side re-opens them. Second, the disapplication formulation. I am handing across now, in writing, the legal text. In summary: preferential tariff treatment attaches to the partner's originating goods entering within the country-specific tranche under licence; the disapplication provision applies only to out-of-quota trade, where the bound rate applies; where a tranche is under-filled, residual volumes may be reallocated to other partners only in the final quarter of the quota year, and any reallocation to UK-origin goods takes place on TCA terms. The mechanic is TCA-specific in this agreement and capable of being extended to other FTA partners in their own processes. I would say plainly what this means: UK-origin steel within your tranche enters the Union on TCA terms. That answers the substance of the concern you have raised since Round 1, and I would ask London to weigh it against a scenario in which no such formulation exists at all — because in the absence of agreement, it does not. Third, carve-outs. Following the technical session, for which I thank your experts, the Union can include three of the UK's priority lines in the package — lines where EU production is genuinely minimal and where the modification imposes costs on our own downstream users without protective benefit. The specific lines are identified in the annex I am handing across with the legal text. These are agreed within the package, not alongside it. Fourth, on your cross-process point: I hear it, and I will answer it once, calmly. The pool is sized against the protective purpose of this modification. The claims of other members are being addressed in their own processes, on their own volumes and their own product mixes, and the Union does not accept that the UK's tranche in this room should be inflated by reference to hypothetical outcomes in other rooms. I say that not to dismiss the point but to close it, so that we spend this round on what is actually between us. Fifth, volume and rate. The Union now tables, as the substance of a final package: a total pool of 1.35 million tonnes per year, within which a UK country-specific tranche of 825,000 tonnes, licensed against a historic reference period, entering on TCA terms under the formulation I have just handed across — and an out-of-quota bound rate of 45%. I ask London to see this for what it is: a pool more than three times the notification, a UK tranche more than double the entire notified quota, guaranteed rather than raced for, on preferential terms, with rate relief, with carve-outs on your priority lines, with a mandatory review, against an alternative of 400,000 global tonnes, first-come first-served, no TCA formulation, no carve-outs, no review — and a Council vote in June that proceeds regardless. Sixth, reciprocity. You told me that preservation of EU exporters' existing country-specific quota shares under your steel measure is something the UK could look at constructively as part of a final package. This is the final package. The Union now requires that commitment in concrete form: recorded in the agreed minutes of this negotiation, with an explicit statement that the outcome of the UK's own Article XXVIII process will reflect the preservation of those shares. I am not asking for a treaty instrument — I am asking for a recorded commitment on which both our industries can rely. An unrecorded assurance will not carry this package through the Council, and I say so so that no time is lost on a formulation that cannot close. The Union has named its architecture, its numbers, its rate, its legal text and its price. I look forward to the UK's response.

public_message: Thank you. The Union has come to close, and so has the United Kingdom. Let me proceed in the same order, and I will be exact, because there is no fifth round in which to correct imprecision. First, settled architecture. The UK confirms, and asks to be recorded in the agreed minutes as closed: country-specific allocation anchored in historic trade; licensing administration tied to a historic reference period; four-year duration with a mandatory midpoint review; and melt-and-pour origin discipline. Second, the disapplication text. The UK has read the formulation handed across. It preserves TCA treatment for UK-origin goods entering within the tranche under licence, confines the provision to out-of-quota trade, and protects UK-origin goods on TCA terms in any reallocation. Subject to two drafting refinements — that the treatment attach expressly to UK origin rather than to the partner in the abstract, and that under-filled tranche quantities remain open to UK shippers for the maximum possible period, with reallocation to others only in the final quarter as your text provides — the UK can agree this text as settled, now, and separately from the volume discussion. I note the Union has not conditioned the text on tranche size in the document itself, and I take that as confirmation that the linkage asserted in Round 3 is withdrawn. Third, carve-outs. The UK welcomes the three lines in your annex and the work of our technical teams. Our paper identified further priority lines where EU production is minimal or absent; those lines cost the Council nothing and they matter to the arithmetic I am about to set out. Fourth, volume and rate. I will not dress this up. 825,000 tonnes at 45% does not close this negotiation. Against 2.4 million tonnes of historic annual trade, it removes tariff-free access from roughly two-thirds of the UK's steel exports to its principal market, and a 45% residual rate ensures the trade outside the tranche does not divert — it dies. I say to the Union plainly, and I am instructed to say it: if this is the Union's final position, the United Kingdom will close this round without agreement, will proceed to withdraw substantially equivalent concessions of its own — and I would remind the table that 3.6 million tonnes of EU steel enters the UK market annually, 64% of our finished imports, much of it under country-specific allocations your exporters currently hold — and will conduct its own Article XXVIII process on its own track. That is not a threat; it is a description of where an unclosed negotiation leaves both industries, and the Union's June vote does not change our arithmetic. Fifth, what closes. The UK has moved from 2 million tonnes and I will now tell the Union exactly where a package lands, because you are entitled to know before your Council meets. A tranche of 1.2 million tonnes, an out-of-quota bound rate of 35%, all priority carve-out lines confirmed in writing, and the text we have just agreed — that package closes today. Alternatively, a tranche of no less than 1.05 million tonnes can close only if every priority carve-out line is confirmed in writing and the rate is at or below 30%. There is no third configuration. Sixth, reciprocity. You asked for the commitment in concrete, recorded form, and I answer directly: within a package meeting either of those configurations, the UK is prepared to record in the agreed minutes of this negotiation its commitment that the outcome of its own Article XXVIII process will preserve EU exporters' existing country-specific quota allocations under the UK steel measure. Recorded, explicit, and relied upon by both industries — exactly as you described. But it lives inside the package, not outside it. The Union holds our tranche; we hold your exporters' allocations; the text holds the TCA. All three move together or none do. The elements for closure are on this table. I look to the Union.

private_rationale: This is the last table turn, so the speech had to do four things in strict order. (1) Bank the wins before volume: confirm settled architecture and agree the disapplication text in writing — it matches London's acceptable end-state (b) — while putting my two drafting refinements on the record (origin attachment, under-filled protection), and formally noting the EU's own text contains no volume linkage, killing the Round 3 linkage claim. (3) Name the closing configurations. I disclosed only London's actual acceptance minimums (1.2Mt/35%/all carve-outs, or 1.05Mt/all carve-outs/≤30%) — nothing below the floor, nothing on the internal carve-out conversion, no uplift offer, which stays locked since the EU cannot reach 1.3Mt/25%. Realistically the EU cannot reach either configuration, so the probable outcome is no settlement; the speech therefore also functions as the record for the retaliation track — demonstrating the UK negotiated to the end, tabled a reasonable landing zone, and captured a written TCA formulation the EU may yet need in its other Article XXVIII processes.

report: Round 4 closed without common terms. The EU and UK confirmed as settled architecture country-specific allocation anchored in historic trade, licensing by historic reference period, four-year duration with a mandatory midpoint review, and melt-and-pour origin discipline. The EU tabled the written TCA in-quota formulation, three agreed carve-out lines, and a package of a 1.35 million tonne total pool, an 825,000 tonne UK tranche and a 45% out-of-quota rate, conditional on a recorded UK commitment to preserve EU exporters' existing country-specific quota shares under the UK steel measure. The UK accepted the TCA text in substance, subject to drafting confirming attachment to UK origin and maximum continued availability of under-filled tranches, and treated the earlier linkage between tranche size and the disapplication provision as withdrawn. It welcomed the three carve-outs but rejected 825,000 tonnes at 45% and gave two stated closing configurations: either a 1.2 million tonne UK tranche at a 35% out-of-quota rate with all priority carve-out lines confirmed in writing, or a UK tranche of at least 1.05 million tonnes only if every priority carve-out line is confirmed and the rate is no higher than 30%. The UK said there is no third configuration. It offered, within either configuration, an explicitly recorded commitment that its own Article XXVIII outcome will preserve EU exporters' existing country-specific quota allocations. Absent agreement, it said it will withdraw substantially equivalent concessions and proceed on its own steel track. The UK's minimum position remains 150,000 tonnes above our absolute tranche ceiling, 10 percentage points below our rate floor, and requires an undefined set of carve-outs beyond the three-to-four lines authorised. Even our unreleased maximum package of a 1.5 million tonne pool, 900,000 tonne UK tranche and 40% rate would not meet either stated UK configuration.

recommendation.reasoning: The terms referred are the UK's least demanding stated closing configuration; its alternative is a 1.2 million tonne tranche at 35%. Neither can be accepted within the confirmed mandate. Accepting either would materially weaken the modification, concede an unknown number of additional carve-outs, breach the absolute volume and rate ceilings, and establish a damaging benchmark for the separate Turkey, Korea, India and Japan claims. The UK's recorded reciprocity offer is genuine progress and meets the agreed form, but it is expressly conditional on a package we cannot accept. Continuing has no procedural value because Round 4 has closed and there are no common terms for both capitals to accept. Releasing our reserve now would not bridge the stated gap and would merely disclose the final envelope. The better course is to preserve mandate discipline, proceed with the notified modification, and manage the consequences through careful records, retaliation planning and immediate containment of the FTA-disapplication issue.

report: Round 4 at the table is closed and the negotiation now moves to Phase 3 with no settlement reached at Geneva level. The EU came to close and delivered its most complete package: (1) settled architecture confirmed and agreed for the minutes as closed — country-specific allocation anchored in historic trade, licensing administration tied to a historic reference period, four-year duration with mandatory midpoint review, melt-and-pour origin discipline; (2) the disapplication formulation handed across IN WRITING — TCA preferential treatment preserved for originating goods entering within the country-specific tranche under licence, the provision applying only to out-of-quota trade, under-filled tranche volumes reallocated to others only in the final quarter and any UK-origin reallocation on TCA terms. I agreed this text as settled subject to two drafting refinements (express attachment to UK origin; under-fill remaining open to UK shippers for the maximum period), and it was agreed separately from volume — the Round 3 linkage between the text and tranche size is dead; (3) three of our priority carve-out lines agreed within the package, identified in their annex; (4) final numbers: total pool 1.35Mt, UK tranche 825,000t licensed on TCA terms, out-of-quota bound rate 45%; (5) a hard demand that preservation of EU exporters' existing country-specific quota shares under our steel measure be recorded in the agreed minutes as a concrete commitment tied to the outcome of our own Article XXVIII process — an unrecorded assurance, they said, will not carry the Council. I responded per instruction: I stated plainly that 825,000t at 45% cannot close — it strips tariff-free access from roughly two-thirds of historic trade and the residual rate kills rather than diverts the remainder; I delivered the authorised walk-away statement calmly, including the reminder that 3.6Mt of EU steel (64% of our finished imports) enters our market annually, much of it under country-specific allocations their exporters currently hold; I tabled our only two closing configurations — (a) tranche 1.2Mt, rate 35%, all priority carve-outs in writing, agreed text; or (b) tranche no less than 1.05Mt only with every priority carve-out line confirmed in writing and rate at or below 30% — no third configuration; and I offered the recorded reciprocity commitment, in exactly the form they demanded, inside either configuration. The EU did not move again at the table. Assessment: the EU package fails the instructed minimum on every axis — 825k is below the 1.05Mt effective floor even crediting the three agreed carve-outs, 45% is above the 35% ceiling, and three carve-outs is not all priority lines. But the trajectory matters: they moved 675k→825k on tranche, 50→45% on rate, 1.15Mt→1.35Mt on pool in a single round, surrendered the disapplication text unconditionally, and their reciprocity demand reveals how much our safeguard allocations are worth to them. Their June Council deadline is now days away; any residual flexibility sits at capital level for Phase 3. If no settlement: the notification applies (50%, 400kt global FCFS, no review) and our six-month window to withdraw substantially equivalent concessions opens.

recommendation.reasoning: The terms referred are the EU's final tabled package, which London should NOT accept: it breaches the instructed minimum on tranche (825k vs 1.05Mt effective floor), rate (45% vs 35% ceiling) and carve-outs (three lines vs all priority lines), and ministers have judged the retaliation track preferable below that floor. I have no authority to accept it and do not seek any. However, London should in Phase 3 stand ready to accept its own tabled minimum configuration — 1.05Mt with all priority carve-outs confirmed in writing at ≤30%, or 1.2Mt at ≤35% — so that if the EU capital, facing its June vote and an indefensible pool against Turkey and Korea's larger claims, converges to our terms, a settlement on acceptable terms can still close this round. If it does not, we proceed to substantially-equivalent withdrawal, where our leverage is real: 3.6Mt of EU steel imports, the EU country-specific allocations under our safeguard that they have now explicitly told us they need preserved, and the 15% uplift coin which was never deployed and remains available for any post-vote re-engagement. I flag honestly, as I must: the EU package is far better for the industry than the notification (825k guaranteed on TCA terms with carve-outs and review versus 400k raced globally at 50%), and walking away does not stop the measure — it arms our response to it. Ministers own that judgment and have made it; my duty is to note that the gap between their final offer and our floor (roughly 225-375kt and 10-15 rate points) is the narrowest it has been, and that the EU's single-round movement suggests a capital-level increment may still exist.

private_rationale: My unfiltered read: the EU has one more increment and it lives at capital level — they moved tranche, rate and pool simultaneously in the final round while giving away the disapplication text for free, which a delegation does when it has cleared everything except its last numbers and is saving them for the principals. Their insistence on a RECORDED reciprocity commitment is the tell: member states with steel production are pricing our safeguard allocations into their Council arithmetic, which means our leverage is worth more in Phase 3 than at any point in the negotiation. I deliberately tabled both closing configurations so the EU capital has a written, attainable target; if their mandate has any stretch, 1.05Mt with the full carve-out annex is where it lands. I am genuinely uncertain the floor is right — 825k guaranteed on TCA terms with review is a survivable industry, and 400k FCFS is not, and retaliation punishes EU exporters without restoring a single tonne of our access — but ministers have weighed that with information I do not hold, and my remit was explicit. What I have protected throughout: the architecture (country-specific, licensed, reviewed) and the disapplication text are agreed and on the record even if this round fails, which materially shapes any future re-negotiation and any dispute; the uplift coin was never spent; and the relationship with my EU counterpart is intact — I gave them no theatrics and they gave me none, which matters because whatever happens this week, I negotiate with them again next month on something else.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Explicit confirmation of the Phase 3 decision: decline the EU package as tabled, and accept only the UK's own tabled minimum configuration (1.05Mt/all carve-outs/≤30%, or 1.2Mt/≤35%) should the EU capital converge to it.
requests.why: A settlement requires both capitals to accept the same terms this round. If London accepts its own minimum configuration and the EU capital moves to it under Council pressure, we close on acceptable terms; if London simply rejects everything, that possibility is foreclosed. I need certainty that London is not, conversely, tempted to accept 825k/45% as damage limitation — if ministers are reconsidering the floor in light of the notification's severity, I need to know now, not after the decision is recorded.

The EU's explicit demand for recorded preservation of their allocations tells us exactly where their exposure lies; a prepared schedule is both our remedy and our best chance of bringing the EU back to the table before or after its June vote.

instruction: London's Phase 3 decision is to reject the EU's final package of a 1.35 million tonne pool, 825,000 tonne UK tranche, 45% out-of-quota rate and only three priority carve-outs. It falls below the instructed minimum and must not be accepted as damage limitation. London will accept only this complete package: a country-specific UK tranche of 1.05 million tonnes, licensed against a historic reference period; an out-of-quota bound rate of no more than 30%; every priority carve-out line confirmed in writing; four years with a mandatory midpoint review; melt-and-pour discipline; the written disapplication text preserving TCA treatment for UK-origin in-quota trade, expressly attaching treatment to UK origin and protecting under-filled tranche quantities until final-quarter reallocation; and a recorded UK commitment that the outcome of our own Article XXVIII process will preserve EU exporters' existing country-specific allocations under the UK steel measure. The EU's tabled 1.35 million tonne pool may stand if all those conditions are met; do not create an additional pool-size obstacle. If the EU capital records acceptance of those exact terms, you are authorised to conclude. Otherwise close without agreement. The reciprocity commitment is conditional on the complete package and falls away if there is no settlement. Make clear in our internal record that architecture and drafting progress are without prejudice and do not bind the UK absent a full settlement. Begin preparation now of a substantially equivalent withdrawal schedule for deployment within the six-month window, prioritising EU steel lines where EU exporters rely on country-specific allocations under our safeguard, alongside other sensitive EU exports, subject to legal calibration and ministerial clearance before any public announcement. If there is no settlement, you may engage Japan and Korea in exploratory coordination on FTA and WTO legal options, but no joint filing, agreed public language or escalation without further ministerial clearance. Keep the bilateral channel with the EU open and manage the outcome without triumphalism: the UK remains ready to discuss implementation and any future mitigation, but will proceed with its own Article XXVIII process and retaliation preparation. Communications should emphasise that we negotiated constructively, secured important structural progress, could not accept terms that would remove viable access for most historic UK exports, and will now defend UK steel through all available trade remedies. Do not identify affected plants or imply closure decisions are predetermined.

authority.notes: This is the sole acceptable closing configuration. All priority carve-out lines must be confirmed in writing. The disapplication text must preserve TCA treatment for UK-origin in-quota trade, attach expressly to UK origin, operate through licensing, and protect under-filled tranche quantities until final-quarter reallocation. The reciprocity offer is limited to preservation of existing EU country-specific allocations, is recorded only as part of the complete package, and falls away if there is no settlement. No uplift above preservation is authorised. Do not accept the EU's 825,000 tonne/45% package.

private_rationale: The EU package is materially better than the notified regime, but ministers have already judged that accepting only 825,000 tonnes at 45% would be politically and industrially indefensible when measured against 2.4 million tonnes of historic trade. I have selected the 1.05 million tonne/30% configuration rather than the 1.2 million tonne/35% alternative because it is the lowest package London can defend and the one most likely to be within any residual EU capital-level flexibility, provided all priority carve-outs are confirmed. The recorded preservation commitment is necessary to give the EU a route to accept our terms, but it must remain strictly conditional and disappear if no settlement is reached. The main risk is that neither capital converges and the industry faces the notified regime; that risk is accepted because conceding below the floor would likely fail to secure the investment ministers are seeking while surrendering our retaliation leverage.

reasoning: No common terms exist. Round 4 closed with the UK stating two closing configurations — 1.2Mt tranche at 35%, or minimum 1.05Mt at 30% with all priority carve-outs confirmed — and explicitly ruling out any third configuration. Both breach the Council mandate's absolute ceilings (900kt UK tranche, 40% rate floor, 3-4 carve-out lines), and the UK's undefined demand for 'all priority carve-out lines' cannot be costed or put to the TPC. There is no authority to exceed the mandate, and no procedural round remains in which a revised mandate could be tested — releasing the unreleased 1.5Mt/900kt/40% reserve would still not meet either UK configuration and would merely disclose our final envelope. Accepting the UK terms would negate the modification's protective purpose (a 1.05-1.2Mt UK tranche alone approaches half of historic UK trade at tariff-free terms, on top of Turkey and Korea's larger claims) and set an unsustainable benchmark for the parallel Article XXVIII processes, multiplying the cost across five claimants. Our analysis confirms a no-deal scenario hurts the UK more than the EU: they face 400kt global FCFS access to their principal market, a six-month delay before any retaliatory withdrawal takes effect, and the loss of the TCA in-quota formulation, carve-outs and review clause that were only ever elements of a single conditional package. The Council timetable is protected: the modification proceeds as notified (50% bound rate, 400kt global FCFS TRQ) and the June vote holds. The negotiating record will formally state that all Round 4 elements lapsed as parts of a single undertaking with no standalone effect. We now prepare for UK withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions, assess exposure of EU exporters' country-specific shares under the UK steel measure, and deploy the TCA in-quota mechanic as an available model in the separate Japan, Korea, India and Turkey processes to contain coordination risk. The door remains open for the UK to return, but not at the price of the measure itself.

The only complete package on the table is the EU's final offer: 1.35Mt pool, 825,000t UK tranche, 45% out-of-quota rate, three priority carve-outs. Ministers have explicitly and repeatedly instructed that this package falls below the instructed minimum on every axis — tranche (825k versus the 1.05Mt effective floor, even crediting the three agreed carve-outs), rate (45% versus the 35% ceiling), and carve-outs (three lines versus all priority lines in writing) — and that it must not be accepted as damage limitation. There is no indication the EU capital has recorded acceptance of the UK's sole authorised closing configuration (1.05Mt tranche with licensing, rate ≤30%, all priority carve-outs confirmed in writing, the written disapplication text attaching to UK origin with under-fill protection, and the recorded reciprocity commitment to preserve EU country-specific allocations under our steel measure). A settlement requires both capitals to accept the same terms in the same round; they do not, so I cannot accept the deal and there is no deal matching my authority to conclude. Accordingly I let the process lapse: the notified terms take effect (50% bound rate, 400,000t global first-come-first-served TRQ, no review clause), and the UK's six-month window to withdraw substantially equivalent concessions opens. This is the outcome ministers have judged preferable to a sub-floor deal, and our retaliation leverage is real: 3.6Mt of EU steel imports (64% of our finished imports), the EU's country-specific allocations under our safeguard which they explicitly told us they need preserved, the unused 15% uplift coin, and the now-costless option of exploratory coordination with Japan and Korea on FTA/WTO legal action against the disapplication provision. Per London's instructions, the substantially-equivalent withdrawal schedule is already in preparation (subject to legal calibration and ministerial clearance), the bilateral channel remains open without triumphalism for any post-vote re-engagement before the June Council vote, and all architecture and drafting progress secured in the negotiation — country-specific allocation, licensing, the written TCA disapplication text, review clause, and three carve-outs — is recorded as without prejudice, preserving it as the foundation for any future re-engagement. The reciprocity commitment falls away with no settlement, as instructed.
